ML based method · Digital twin: five years, 579 wells

Five years of history for every well, and a ML forecaster that reads each well's own physics.

The company's real records cover two weeks. Forecasting a week ahead needs years: several monsoons, several dry seasons, and the slow decline in between. So we built a physics twin of the fleet, five years long, and tested the forecaster on it blind. The one-year digital twin used elsewhere on this site is the final year of this same twin.

What we have, what we built, what we test

Vendor export

A 14.5-day export

579 wells, 15–29 July 2026, in the vendor's file format. Its level values are demonstration data: it gives us the format and each well's operating pattern, not a real level history.

Digital twin

A five-year twin of the fleet

579 simulated wells, hour by hour, August 2021 to July 2026, driven by real IMD rainfall, with hidden traits, interference between wells, sensor noise and faults. It writes files in the exact vendor format.

Known answer

The pipeline, run blind

The forecaster sees only the files and public rainfall. Its forecasts are scored against the twin's hidden truth, which the model code is checked never to read. When real data arrives, the same pipeline recalibrates each well on it.

How the twin was generated

A simulator, not a dataset. It draws hidden traits for each well, then integrates its water level hour by hour under rain, pumping, neighbours and a sensor model. One seed reproduces it exactly; the build takes under two minutes.

1 · Each well's hidden traits

Every well is a two-store reservoir: a fast store that the pump draws down and that recovers when it stops, and a slow store, the resting level of the surrounding rock. Its traits are drawn once and never shown to the model: resting level (median 55 m), recovery pace τ (median 8 h), drawdown coefficient a (median 0.4 m per m³), pump rate and efficiency, intake depth, and a fracture zone below which drawdown steepens.

2 · Real rain, delayed recharge

IMD gridded daily rainfall for the city, so every monsoon and every dry spell in the twin happened. A soil bucket takes the rain; its overflow reaches the aquifer after a per-well delay of 5–30 days and lifts the resting level. A slow drain and a dry-season decline pull it back down.

3 · Pumping and dry runs

Each well pumps on its own pattern from the export: sessions per day, start hours, durations, scaled by season and cut on supply-outage days. When the level reaches the intake the pump runs dry: discharge collapses, the controller locks it out, the session is logged as cancelled. Five years produced 38,882 dry-run events in 113 wells.

4 · Wells that affect each other

A hidden graph of 733 edges links neighbours. Water flows along each edge in proportion to the difference in the two wells' drawdowns, so a pumping well drags its neighbours down and an idle one lets them recover. The model never knows who is connected to whom.

5 · What the sensors see

The true level is never written to the observed files. The forecaster gets what the vendor's sensors would record: a level at the start and stop of each session with ±0.2 m noise, 0.5 % outlier readings, 3 % missing days, telemetry every five minutes, and faults on 10 % of wells: stuck level, slow drift, spikes, a flowmeter reading double.

6 · The twin's own gate

Before any model was trained the twin had to pass six automated checks: file format, physics (drawdown positive, idle wells recover, monsoons lift levels), the observation model, isolation of the truth, and fidelity to the real export (sessions per day, duration, cadence, discharge all within band). Then it was frozen.

Output: 1.64 million sessions and 54.6 million telemetry rows over five years; the final year also as 1,158 CSV files byte-compatible with the real export; 25 million hourly true levels, traits, edges and the dry-run log kept as hidden truth.

The forecaster in five steps

A physics core makes the first guess; a learning layer corrects it; calibration makes the range honest.

  1. Read each well's physics from its own records. Recovery segments (pump off) give τ and the resting level; drawdown segments (pump on) give a. Readings far from a 61-day median are dropped before fitting. 216 features per well-day, all from the observed files.
  2. Two equations give the first guess for each of the next seven days.
    hrest = hs + (hstop − hs) · e−rest/τ
    Recovery, pump off: the gap to the resting level closes at the well's own pace τ.
    deepest = hrest + a · Q · τ · (1 − e−t/τ)
    Drawdown, pump on: a session of length t at rate Q deepens the level toward a limit set by a, Q and τ.
  3. A learning layer corrects what the physics leaves out. Gradient-boosted models (LightGBM) predict the difference between the observed level and the physics core, for each day ahead and for the 10th, 50th and 90th percentile: 21 models. Because they predict a correction, not a level, the physics carries the forecast when history is short and the models take over as evidence accumulates.
  4. Calibrate the range. Conformal calibration widens or narrows the band, per day ahead and per season, until on the calibration year the 80 % band holds 80 % of readings. The offsets are then applied unchanged to the test year.
  5. Turn levels into decisions. The drawdown equation is inverted against each well's threshold to give a safe pumping volume for the day and the week; a risk model blends the level-forecast probability with a classifier trained on the well's own dry-run history to raise the weekly dry-run flag.

The known-answer test

Because the twin's traits are hidden, we can ask whether the features recover them from the sensor files alone: the same step the pipeline will perform on real wells.

Recovery pace τ, fitted vs true0.75rank correlation; target ≥ 0.70
Drawdown coefficient a, fitted vs true0.95rank correlation; target ≥ 0.70
Size of a, fitted over true0.86inside the 0.85–1.15 band
Look-ahead cells out of 8,200050 rows rebuilt with the future removed: identical

Estimating a took two attempts. A straight-line fit read it 36 % low, because long sessions flatten as the level saturates; a fit that follows the flattening corrected it. On real wells nobody knows the true a, so that bias would have gone unnoticed. Catching it is what a known-answer test is for.

How it was tested honestly

SplitTrain August 2021 – July 2024; choose thresholds, blend weights and band widths on August 2024 – July 2025; test once on August 2025 – July 2026, with a forecast every week. Unseen wells116 wells (20 %) held out of training entirely and scored separately. BaselinesAssume the level stays where it is today; a seasonal guess; the well's running mean; the physics core alone. Three gatesTwin, features and forecaster each pass an automated test suite before the next stage starts; the forecaster's gate checks 13 thresholds fixed in the plan before any model was trained. Truth firewallNothing in the feature or model code reads the hidden truth; a test greps for it, and the feature build is re-run with the truth hidden to prove it.
Honest status

Every figure from this stage is on the twin, with ±0.2 m level noise. No real level measurement was used. The twin also has known limits: it is a two-store reservoir with random traits, not real hydrogeology; one rain cell serves the whole city; nobody in it reacts to a low level; and its recharge was too generous in this iteration, which is being corrected. What the stage proves is the method: that the pipeline reads a well's behaviour from its files and forecasts it a week ahead with an honest range.

See what it achieved →

Borewell Forecast is a proof of concept for forecasting groundwater levels in Bengaluru borewells. Results are labelled by where the data came from: vendor export (15 days, July 2026, in the vendor's real format but with demonstration water-level values), synthetic test system (450 simulated wells with a known answer) or digital twin (a physics-based simulation of the 579 wells over a year). No real water-level measurement has been used yet, and nothing here is yet a validated field forecast.
